title.narrative: Output 6.3. Increased capacity of member States to develop gender-responsive legislation, policies and measures for a world of work free from violence and harassment

description.narrative:
Awareness-raising activities on C190 were conducted by the DÝSK Confederation and affiliated members such as DÝSK TEKSTÝL in the textile sector, the TÜRK-METAL union, and the TEKSÝF union, an affiliated member of the TÜRK-ÝÞ Confederation in the metal and textile sectors respectively. As a result, several trade unions included provisions on violence and harassment and, in particular, on gender-based violence and harassment in their collective bargaining agreements. For instance, the CA signed in January 2021 by TEZKOOP-ÝÞ – an affiliated member of TÜRK-ÝÞ in the office and commerce sector – with the Chambers of Engineers and Architects, which now includes disciplinary measures in cases of violence and harassment.
On the occasion of DÝSK's General Assembly in February 2020, the Confederation issued a for ratification of C190, and it was agreed to produce and disseminated awareness-raising materials on C190 and its ratification. Moreover, in August 2020, the Memur-Sen Confederation (Confederation of Public Servants Trade Unions) incorporated into its congress a session on violence in the world of work, which resulted in increased awareness.
In November 2020, Automotive company Karsan, an affiliate of employers' organisation MESS/TISK, adopted, through ILO's support, a Zero Tolerance to Violence at Work Policy – aligned with C190. Employees were provided with training via the online platform ILO Academy. The company established partnerships with public institutions as well as CSOs in order to ensure the full implementation of the policy. In March 2020, KARSAN join Bursa Network on Women's Empowerment Principles (WEPs) and became a WEPs signatory. KARSAN won 2021 Silver Stevie Winner award (one of the most prestigious Human Resources awards in the world) at the category of Success in Leadership Development for Women (https://www.karsan.com/ua/presse/awards-ua/karsans-website-wins-two-stevie-awards-award-ua). The ILO, through the technical cooperation project "More and Better Jobs for Women" funded by Sweden, provided extensive support to constituents in their efforts towards the ratification and implementation of C190. In particular, the ILO contributed to the development and rollout of numerous awareness-raising activities, events and programmes on the prevention and elimination of violence and harassment in the world of work. ILO actively engaged in international campaign for the 2020 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence and advocated for adoption of the C190. ILO also translated the ILO-UN Women "Handbook Addressing Violence and Harassment against Women in the World of Work" into Turkish and widely disseminated it through social media and other channels, with a view to increasing the knowledge of the constituents and of the general public on issues related to violence and harassment.
Furthermore, ILO provided technical support to enterprises through the "Gender Equality Model at Enterprises Programme". This programme aims at increase capacity for the effective mainstreaming of gender equality issues, including violence and harassment, into human resources policies and practices at the enterprise level. In particular, and upon request, the ILO supported the effective implementation of this Module in KARSAN factory for the last two years. This technical support has been pivotal in developing and adopting the Zero Tolerance to Violence Policy and in supporting its implementation. The ILO also provided access to relevant training through its ILO Academy online website (https://www.karsan.com/en/press/current-news/karsan-is-the-first-corporation-to-receive-the-zero-tolerance-against-violence-training-provided-by-ilo-academy). The recent Silver Stevie Winner award received by Karsan confirmed the key progress achieved through ILO's contributions.

description.narrative:
The International Labour Organization (ILO) Office for Turkey, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Union of Municipalities of Turkey (UMT) signed a protocol on 24 June 2021 to extend the early childhood care and education (ECCE) services provided by municipalities in order to alleviate the burden of care on women, and contribute to increasing women's employment.
In consultation with the government's related entities and social partners, the report on "Supporting Women's Employment through Institutional Collaboration on Early Childhood Care and Education (2021)" was prepared in 2020. The Report proposes enhancement of three options for childcare services, namely Organized Industry Zone (OIZ) Practice in cooperation with employers, Municipal Practice led by municipalities, and Labour Union Practice by unions organized at workplace. Based on recommendations on municipal practice of the report which was prepared by contribution of the metropolitan municipalities of the pilot provinces of the project and, the Union of Municipalities of Turkey a technical working group composed of municipalities, government's related institutions and social partners was established to extend the scope of early childhood care and education services provided by municipalities though revision of policy and legal framework municipalities in 2021. The ILO established an inclusive social dialogue platform in order to promote the recognition, redistribution and reduction of time spent in unpaid care work. ILO raised awareness on gender gap in unpaid care work in the platform. ILO, in cooperation with EBRD provided technical support for comprehensive examination of the legal and policy framework regulating early childhood care and education (ECCE) services, roles of service providers, and good practices in Turkey and in the world. Regarding the findings and the recommendations of the report, the ILO made constituents' ownership increased through regular consultation and soliciting the contributions and views of public agencies, workers' and employers' organizations, local governments, private sector and civil society.
Based on demands of the Union of Municipalities and the municipalities in the pilot provinces of the project, the ILO organised the workshop to discuss on challenges and opportunities of municipalities for providing early child care services in 2020. With reference to outcomes of the workshop, the ILO advocated strengthening roles and responsibilities of municipalities for providing early child care services especially to households in which unemployed or informally working women lives.

Output 6.2. Increased capacity of the ILO constituents to strengthen policies and strategies to promote and ensure equal opportunities, participation and treatment between women and men, including equal remuneration for work of equal value

description.narrative:
The Public Employment Agency of Turkey , in consultation with social partners, initiated a revision process of the National Action Plan (NAP) on Women's Employment in order to support women's access to decent work opportunities and a National Technical Team with tripartite structure was re-established in 2020 for this purpose.
The Department of Employment Policies (under the Ministry of Labour and Social Security) and workers' and employers' organizations (totally 21 organization involved) conducted the ILO Participatory Gender Audit at their own institutions and developed Road Maps between 2019 and 2021. Some of trade unions, among those of whom implemented the Participatory Gender Audit, revised their statutes from gender equality perspective.
Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions (DISK) added "gender equality" angle to its Code as one of the main objectives and principles of the Confederation in 2020. Additionally, the Confederation recognized "Women Representatives Committee" and "Regional Women Representatives Committee" as one of the Confederation's Organs.
BIRLESIK-METAL Trade Union (affiliated member of DISK in metal sector) adopted a General Assembly Resolution on gender equality and made changes in its Code in line with this Resolution. The Resolution aims to improve gender equality in union and their organized workplaces. It also stated that the trade union enhances its efforts for women access to decision making mechanisms. Additionally, the Resolution includes measures for improvement of women's working conditions with a special focus on work –life balance especially distribution of care responsibilities and stopping violence against women in the world of work.
Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat) published the "Measuring the Gender Wage Gap: Turkey Case" report that analyses the Gender Wage Gap in Turkey with technical support of ILO. ILO provided technical support to the establishment of a tripartite National Technical Team in 2020 to ensure implementation of social dialogue mechanism in revision process of the National Action Plan. ILO conducted capacity and needs assessment study and based on the findings of the study, training programmes and materials were developed and organised by ILO.
Further, ILO increased awareness on C100 and on the gender pay gap (GPG); and organized a series of consultation meetings for recognition of gender wage gap in the country; and also established a strong partnership with Turkish Statistic Institution (TURSTAT) to calculate GPG with a new approach. ILO provided technical support to TURSTAT on measuring gender pay gap with reference to ILO global approach applied in the ILO "Global Wage Report 2018/19". Additionally, ILO contributed raising awareness of private sector on gender pay gap and improving capacities of enterprises on ways of rectifying pay differentials between women and men at enterprises level. As a part of "Gender Equality Model at Enterprises", gender pay gap is one of the five priorities of the model. During the implementation of the Model, special training and consultation sessions were carried out at KARSAN factory in 2020 and 2021.
ILO established an expert pool of national gender experts on Participatory Gender Audit for conducting the "ILO Participatory Gender Audit (PGA)" of the constituents. ITC ILO conducted ToT training and provided consultancy support in 2020 which was followed up by ILO technical support and guidance to all partners involved in the participatory gender audit. Additionally, ILO supported trade unions to raise awareness on gender equality among their members through delivering trainings, workshops and conferences. In response to the pandemic, ILO designed the first digital training on "Zero Tolerance to Violence" 2021 publicly available at the ILO Academy.

title.narrative: 6.2.1. Number of member States with policies to promote substantive equality of opportunity and treatment between women and men in the world of work, and strategies for their implementation
Output A.1. More accurate and sustainable statistics on decent work using the latest statistical standards

description.narrative:
The national statistics authority (the Turkish Statistical Institute, TurkStat) has revised the methodology utilised for the calculation of the gender pay gap. They accepted to start using the SILC (Statistics on Income and Living Conditions survey) to accompany the SES (Structure of Earnings Survey). The result is an enhanced coverage of employees. The SES only covers formal employees in companies with more than 10 employees excluding the agricultural sector and the public administration (among other, less relevant, exceptions). The SILC, in turn, covers all employees, formal and informal, in both the public and the private sector. Increased representation on national statistics of the most vulnerable ones is the key result that is extracted.
In line with increasing awareness with regards vulnerable groups, TurkStat have also published pay gaps by occupation, economic activity and ownership of the workplace (public/private). In addition, they have produced so-called "factor-weighted" pay gaps which, in a nutshell, aims at correcting the composition of the workforce to produce more accurate pay gaps. At last, TurkStat has also calculated a so-called motherhood gap, to show that the distance in wages between men and women is increased among parents than among singles. The ILO contribution has been twofold, technical and influential. With regards to the former, the ILO prepared a report explaining the different coverage achieved by the surveys that could be utilised for the calculation of the gender pay gap (LFS, SILC, SES, HBS) and the consequences for the gap of using each of these surveys. In addition, the ILO provided an expert to work together with TurkStat and developed the final report where the pay gaps mentioned in the "results achieved" section were published.
On the awareness raising side (or influential side) the ILO organized a panel discussion to explain to a wide audience the importance of measuring gaps correctly, how to interpret them and what measures are being used in other countries to tackle it. In addition, the ILO organized a technical workshop with attendees coming from relevant ministries and institutions (including TurkStat) to show the importance of survey choice when measuring the pay gap and the consequences in terms of representativity that carry the use of an enterprise survey like the SES.
In addition, several seminars were organized by the team to foster awareness raising around the country, explaining the results achieved by the new methodology and their implications for women.
